literal: He died young; posthumously made Scattered Cavalier Attendant.
idiomatic: He died young and was posthumously made Scattered Cavalier Attendant.

literal: You — younger brother — Xi, Prince Wenzhuang of Zhongshan
idiomatic: You's younger brother: Xi, Prince Wenzhuang of Zhongshan

literal: (Attached sons: Jingxian, Zhongxian, Shuxian, Shuren / Shuren — son — Lin)
idiomatic: (Sons: Jingxian, Zhongxian, Shuxian, Shuren; Shuren's son: Lin)

literal: You's younger brother Xi, styled Zhenxing.
idiomatic: You's brother Xi, courtesy name Zhenxing.

literal: He loved learning, was handsome and bright with literary talent, his fame resounding in the age—yet he was frivolous, rash, and restless.
idiomatic: He loved books, was brilliant and literary, famed in his day—yet frivolous and restless.

literal: Ying deeply worried he was not fit to preserve the house; he often wished to disinherit him and establish the fourth son Lüe as heir, but clan opinion would not listen, and Lüe also firmly declined—thereupon he stopped.
idiomatic: Ying feared he would ruin the house and tried to make his fourth son Lüe heir; the clan refused, and Lüe refused too—so he desisted.

literal: He began his career as Secretariat Attendant; in the second year of Yanxi he inherited the fief, was promoted in succession to Acting Director of Palace Construction, made Vice Director of the Court for Imperial Sacrifices and Palace Attendant Yellow Gate Attendant-in-ordinary, and soon transferred to Minister of the Household.
idiomatic: He entered service as a secretariat attendant, inherited in Yanxi year 2, rose through construction and ritual posts to Yellow Gate attendant-in-ordinary, then Minister of the Household.

literal: At the time Area Commander-in-chief Yu Zhong held power.
idiomatic: Yu Zhong, area commander-in-chief, held the government.

literal: Xi was Yu Zhong's son-in-law; therefore within the year he was suddenly promoted.
idiomatic: Xi was Zhong's son-in-law and was promoted with unnatural speed.

literal: Soon he was made Pacify-the-West General and Eastern Qinzhou Inspector, advanced in title to Pacify-the-Qin General and Director of the Palace Library.
idiomatic: Soon he was Pacify-the-West General and Eastern Qinzhou inspector, then Pacify-the-Qin General and palace librarian.

literal: Soon with that general's title he was given Xiangzhou Inspector.
idiomatic: He was then made inspector of Xiangzhou under the same rank.

literal: Xi entered to govern in the seventh month; that day great wind and cold rain—more than twenty men froze to death, and several tens of donkeys and horses.
idiomatic: He took office in the seventh month; that day a gale and cold rain killed more than twenty men and dozens of pack animals.

literal: Xi heard of his grandfather's earlier affair and hated it in his heart.
idiomatic: He brooded on his grandfather's fate.

literal: Maggots also bred in his courtyard.
idiomatic: Maggots bred in his courtyard.

literal: Earlier, Xi and his brothers had all been favored by Prince Yi of Qinghe; when Liu Teng and Yuan Cha cut off the Two Palaces and forged an edict to kill Yi, Xi thereupon raised troops and memorialized: "Your servant has heard that safety and danger have no constancy—times have their rest and decline.
idiomatic: Once he and his brothers had been close to Prince Yi of Qinghe; when Liu Teng and Yuan Cha walled off the palaces and forged an edict to kill Yi, Xi raised troops and wrote: "Safety and danger have no fixed hour.

literal: Your servant early belonged to a bright age, late met many hardships.
idiomatic: I was born to brightness and met only hardship.

literal: Since the imperial foundation has been lush and nine leaves have borne glory, Gaozu and Shizong, emblems bright succeeding one another.
idiomatic: Nine generations have flourished since Gaozu and Shizong.

literal: The Empress Dowager's sacred reverence comes from Heaven, virtue equal to Ma and Deng;
idiomatic: The Empress Dowager's virtue equals Ma and Deng;

literal: His Majesty's divine wisdom inherits the throne, divine mirror shining far.
idiomatic: His Majesty rules with divine sight.

literal: Within the four seas all is calm; the eight directions return to transformation.
idiomatic: The realm is calm; the eight directions submit.

literal: Yet Area Commander Yuan Cha, relying on favor through outside kin, greedily honored at the left and right, wolf heart—fed full, he turns to bite.
idiomatic: Yet Yuan Cha, favored through kin, sits at the emperor's side with a wolf's heart—fed full, he bites.

literal: He made the Two Palaces cut off, warm greetings and care lacking in ritual; again the Grand Tutor Prince Yi of Qinghe was slaughtered across.
idiomatic: He walled off the Two Palaces, ended the rites of filial care, and had Prince Yi of Qinghe butchered.

literal: He made loyal ministers and martyrs lose spirit at the court gate;
idiomatic: Loyal men lost heart at the gate;

literal: kin and worthies of the clan, anger and hate within and without.
idiomatic: kin and worthies seethed within and without.

literal: Pointing at deer and calling them horses—who can go beyond this?
idiomatic: Calling deer horses—who can outdo that?

literal: Wang Mang and Dong Zhuo forcing power—compared with this, no likeness.
idiomatic: Wang Mang and Dong Zhuo beside this are nothing.

literal: Your servant looks up at the cloud gate, weeping blood while alive—if fine grass is not cleared it will become rank growth; how much more when Cha's rebellion is thus—who can bear it!
idiomatic: I weep blood beneath the cloud gate—uncut grass becomes a jungle; Cha's crime is worse—who can bear it?

literal: Your servant, bearing branch and calyx of the tree, thinks to exhaust strength and life, smash head and butcher liver—sweet as shepherd's purse.
idiomatic: I am of the imperial branch and will spend life and liver gladly.

literal: Now I have raised righteous troops in fact, armor eight myriad; the great host already advances, civil and military vie to be first—with Bingzhou Inspector Prince Hui of Chengyang, Hengzhou Inspector Prince Yuan of Guangyang, Xuzhou Inspector Prince of Qi Xiao Baoyin, and others, all to set out together on the fourteenth of this month.
idiomatic: I raise eight myriad men in arms; with Prince Hui of Chengyang, Prince Yuan of Guangyang, and Xiao Baoyin of Qi I march on the fourteenth.

literal: I hope to lean on the spirits of the ancestors, bow and exhaust the righteous men's lives, sweep the vicious and ugly, and again clear the capital.
idiomatic: By our ancestors' shades we will scour the villains and clear the capital.

literal: Your servant personally commands the three armies, stars hurrying to the crisis, placing troops at Warm City, lying low to hear Heaven's command.
idiomatic: I lead three armies to Warm City and wait on Heaven's word.

literal: Dukes, ministers, and aides—some famed for loyalty through generations, some long cherishing grace and regard—if you can join strength and cut down Yuan Cha, so that the Empress Dowager and His Majesty may gladly face one another, your servant will at once unarm and disband the host and go to answer at the court gate.
idiomatic: Princes and ministers famed for loyalty—join me, cut down Cha, restore the Empress Dowager and the Son of Heaven to one another, and I will lay down arms at the gate.

literal: Though your servant's talent falls short of men of old, my place is the frontier screen of the realm—how can I sit and watch vicious ugliness and vainly receive glory and salary!"
idiomatic: I hold a frontier fief—how can I watch villains and still draw salary?"

literal: Xi's troops had risen only ten days when his Chief Clerk Liu Yuanzhang, Vice Director You Jing, and Wei Commandery Governor Li Xiaoyi led the people of the cities, beating drums and clamoring as they entered, killed more than forty of Xi's attendants, seized Xi, placed him on a high tower, and together with his sons and younger brothers.
idiomatic: Ten days after he rose, his chief clerk, vice director, and Wei governor led the townsfolk in, killed forty of his men, seized Xi and his sons, and held them in a tower.

literal: Cha sent Left Vice Director of the Masters of Writing Lu Tong to behead him in the Ye street and sent his head to the capital.
idiomatic: Cha sent Lu Tong to behead him in the streets of Ye and sent his head to the capital.

literal: From the first Xi's consort the Lady Yu knew Xi would fail and did not follow his plot; from the beginning she wept without cease until Xi's death.
idiomatic: His wife Lady Yu knew he would fail, refused his plot, and wept without stop until he died.

literal: At execution Xi composed a five-character poem and showed it to his clerks and officials: "Righteousness truly moves the gentleman; the lord's disgrace—death for the loyal minister.
idiomatic: Facing death he wrote five lines for his staff: "Righteousness stirs the noble heart; a lord's shame calls the loyal man to die.

literal: How to make clear this integrity? About to untie seven feet of body."
idiomatic: How shall I show this faith? I give up seven feet of flesh."

literal: Parting from close friends he said: "All my life one square inch of heart, earnestness entrusted to the knowing friend.
idiomatic: To friends he said: "All my life one heart I gave to friends.

literal: From now one melting away—grief without limit."
idiomatic: Now it melts away—grief without end."

literal: Xi, being noble among the frontier princes, moreover had literature; he loved the strange and cherished the different, formed ties with great and handsome men, his air very lofty, his name beautiful in the age—elders before and juniors after, many came to his gate.
idiomatic: A frontier prince and a man of letters, he sought out brilliant company; the age praised him, and many came to his door.

literal: When Xi first went to govern Ye, talented literary men Yuan Fan, Li Yan, Li Shenjun, the Wang Song brothers, Pei Jingxian, and others all saw him off at River Bridge, composing poems in farewell.
idiomatic: When he left for Ye, Yuan Fan, Li Shenjun, the Wang brothers, Pei Jingxian, and others saw him off at River Bridge with poems.

literal: When Xi was about to die he again wrote to old friends: "I and my younger brother both received the Empress Dowager's knowing encounter; elder brother held a great province, younger brother then entered attendance—earnest words and color, grace like a loving mother.
idiomatic: Before death he wrote to friends: "My brother and I were cherished by the Empress Dowager—he in a great province, I at court—treated like sons.

literal: Now the Empress Dowager is deposed in the North Palace; the Grand Tutor Prince Yi of Qinghe was slaughtered across; the lord is young, alone in the front hall.
idiomatic: Now she is confined in the North Palace, Prince Yi was butchered, and the boy emperor sits alone.

literal: Lord and kin thus—I cannot be at peace; therefore I lead soldiers and people to raise great righteousness under Heaven.
idiomatic: I could not rest; I raised arms in the name of righteousness.

literal: But my strength and wit shallow and short—soon I was seized; above I shame the court, below I fail my friends.
idiomatic: My wits were short; I was seized at once—shame to the court, shame to you.

literal: Originally it was fame and duty that moved my heart—I could not do otherwise; guts streaming, head smashed—what more is there to say!
idiomatic: Duty drove me; guts spill—what more can I say?

literal: In old times Li Si remembered the yellow dog of Shangcai; Lu Ji thought of the crane's cry at Huating—was it not because illusion has no bound, once gone never to return?
idiomatic: Li Si remembered Shangcai's yellow dog; Lu Ji the crane at Huating—gone, never back.

literal: Now I wish to face the autumn moon, meet the spring wind, lean on fragrant grass, shade flowering trees, broadly summon famous guests, compose poems on the Luo shore—can it be obtained?
idiomatic: I will not face the moon, the wind, the grass, the trees, or poems on the Luo again.

literal: All you gentlemen, each respect your proper conduct; for the state and for the body, well urge fame and integrity, establish merit and affairs—for the body alone—what have I to say!
idiomatic: Live for the state and for yourselves; make merit; I have no more words."

literal: People of the time pitied him.
idiomatic: Men pitied him.

literal: Also, before Prince Cheng of Ren's death, Xi dreamed someone told him: "Ren will die.
idiomatic: Before Prince Cheng of Ren died, Xi dreamed a voice said, "Ren will die.

literal: Two hundred days after his death, you too will not escape.
idiomatic: Two hundred days later you will not escape.

literal: If you do not believe it, try looking at Ren's house."
idiomatic: If you doubt it, look at Ren's mansion."

literal: In the dream Xi looked back at Ren's residence; the walls on four sides collapsed—no remaining parapet.
idiomatic: In the dream he saw Ren's walls fall on every side to the ground.

literal: Xi hated it; waking, he told those close to him.
idiomatic: He woke in dread and told his kin.

literal: When Xi died, it was indeed as in the dream.
idiomatic: When he died, it was as the dream had said.

literal: The three brothers, whenever they followed Ying on campaign, in the army were greedy and violent; sometimes in welcoming surrender and pursuing the defeated they would even behead the innocent, often adding to the head count to make merit reports.
idiomatic: All three followed Ying to war and grew greedy and cruel—sometimes killing the innocent among surrendering fugitives to pad their body counts.

literal: Also in Yu Zhong's framing of Guo Zuo and Pei Zhi, Zhong's mind had not yet decided to kill them—through Xi's urging and encouragement they came to the extreme penalty; the age considered it a wrong.
idiomatic: When Yu Zhong framed Guo Zuo and Pei Zhi, Xi urged him on to execution—the world called it injustice.

literal: When Xi's calamity came, debaters held there was retribution.
idiomatic: When Xi fell, men said it was retribution.

literal: When the Empress Dowager Ling restored government, she posthumously made him bearer of the staff, Area Commander of military affairs in Ji, Ding, Ying, Xiang, and You provinces, Grand General, Grand Commandant, Ji Province Inspector, added one thousand households to his original fief, posthumous title Prince Wenzhuang.
idiomatic: When Empress Dowager Ling returned to power, she restored him as commander of five provinces, Grand General, Grand Commandant, added a thousand households, and titled him Prince Wenzhuang.

literal: The eldest son Jingxian, next Zhongxian, next Shuxian—all were killed together with Xi.
idiomatic: Jingxian, Zhongxian, and Shuxian died with him.

literal: Later Jingxian was posthumously made Central Army General and Qingzhou Inspector, buried with princely rites;
idiomatic: Jingxian was later made Central Army General and Qingzhou inspector and buried as a prince;

literal: Zhongxian, Left General and Yanzhou Inspector;
idiomatic: Zhongxian as Left General and Yanzhou inspector;

literal: Shuxian, Right General and Qizhou Inspector.
idiomatic: Shuxian as Right General and Qizhou inspector.

literal: Shuxian's younger brother Shuren, because he was young, was spared whole, and with his mother the Lady Yu was moved to Shuozhou.
idiomatic: Young Shuren was spared and sent to Shuozhou with his mother Lady Yu.

literal: At the beginning of Xiaochang the Empress Dowager Ling ordered Shuren to return to the capital, restored his property and residence, and he inherited the former title.
idiomatic: In Xiaochang year 1 Ling ordered Shuren home, restored his estate, and let him inherit.

literal: He was made General Who Subdues the Barbarians and Regular Attendant, Direct Transmission.
idiomatic: He became General Who Subdues the Barbarians and regular attendant for direct transmission.

literal: At the beginning of Xiaozhuang he met disaster at Heyin; posthumously made Guard General, Equal in Honor to the Three Dukes, and Bingzhou Inspector.
idiomatic: At Xiaozhuang's accession he died at Heyin and was posthumously made Guard General with honor equal to the Three Dukes and inspector of Bingzhou.

literal: His son Lin inherited.
idiomatic: His son Lin succeeded.

literal: When Qi received the mandate, titles were reduced by precedent.
idiomatic: When Qi took the throne, the fief was reduced as custom required.

literal: Xi — younger brother — You
idiomatic: Xi's younger brother: You

literal: (Attached son: Shibo)
idiomatic: (Son: Shibo)

literal: Xi's younger brother You, styled Huixing.
idiomatic: Xi's brother You, courtesy name Huixing.

literal: From Outer Palace Attendant he was gradually promoted to Regular Attendant, Crown Prince Central Palace Attendant, General Who Subdues the Barbarians, Vice Director of the Court for Imperial Guards, and went out as Right General and Southern Qinzhou Inspector.
idiomatic: He rose from outer attendant to crown prince's central attendant, Guard vice director, then Right General and Southern Qinzhou inspector.

literal: Cha beheaded him in Qizhou; wife and children were not implicated.
idiomatic: Cha executed him in Qizhou; his family was spared.

literal: Posthumously made Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry and Yongzhou Inspector; later posthumously made Equal in Honor to the Three Dukes, enfeoffed as founding Earl of Duchang with eight hundred households, posthumous title Gong.
idiomatic: He was posthumously made Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry and Yongzhou inspector, later equal to the Three Dukes, founding Earl of Duchang with eight hundred households, titled Gong.

literal: His son Shibo inherited.
idiomatic: His son Shibo succeeded.

literal: Palace Attendant.
idiomatic: Shibo served as palace attendant.

literal: When Qi received the mandate, titles were reduced by precedent.
idiomatic: When Qi took the throne, the title was reduced by precedent.

literal: You — younger brother — Lüe, Prince Wenzhen of Dongping
idiomatic: You's younger brother: Lüe, Prince Wenzhen of Dongping

literal: (Attached son: Jingshi)
idiomatic: (Son: Jingshi)

literal: You's younger brother Lüe, styled Junxing.
idiomatic: You's brother Lüe, courtesy name Junxing.

literal: His talent and air were inferior to Xi's, yet he had a reputation for harmony and depth.
idiomatic: Less brilliant than Xi, he was known for calm depth.

literal: From Outer Palace Attendant he was gradually promoted to Feathered Forest Supervisor, Regular Attendant Scattered Cavalier, Champion General, and Palace Attendant Yellow Gate Attendant-in-ordinary.
idiomatic: He rose through the feathered forest, scattered cavalier, champion general, to Yellow Gate attendant-in-ordinary.

literal: After Prince Yi of Qinghe died, Cha demoted Lüe to deputy commander of Huaishuo Garrison.
idiomatic: After Prince Yi's death, Cha demoted him to deputy at Huaishuo Garrison.

literal: Before he could go to his post, Xi raised troops and letters went back and forth between him and Lüe.
idiomatic: Before he took post, Xi rebelled and letters passed between the brothers.

literal: Soon Xi failed; Lüe then traveled in secret, entrusting himself to an old acquaintance, Interior Minister of Henei Shi Bin.
idiomatic: When Xi fell, Lüe fled in secret to Shi Bin, interior minister of Henei.

literal: Shi Bin then made a reed raft; by night he and Lüe together crossed the Meng Ford and went to Li Faguang of Tunliu in Shangdang.
idiomatic: Bin built a reed raft; by night they crossed the Meng Ford to Li Faguang at Tunliu in Shangdang.

literal: Faguang had always been thick in faith and righteousness; gladly he received him.
idiomatic: Faguang, a man of faith, welcomed him gladly.

literal: Lüe's old acquaintance Diao Shuang was then Western River Governor; Lüe again went to him.
idiomatic: Lüe's friend Diao Shuang was Western River governor; Lüe went to him next.

literal: He stopped more than a year; Shuang then ordered his nephew Chang to send Lüe in secret to slip south of the Yangzi.
idiomatic: He stayed a year; Shuang's nephew Chang smuggled him south of the Yangzi.

literal: Xiao Yan treated him with great courtesy and respect; he enfeoffed Lüe as Prince of Zhongshan with a household of one thousand and made him Xuancheng Governor.
idiomatic: Xiao Yan honored him, made him Prince of Zhongshan with a thousand households, and Xuancheng governor.

literal: Soon Xuzhou Inspector Yuan Faseng held the south of the city and rebelled; gentry and commoners within the province were all compelled by Faseng.
idiomatic: Soon Yuan Faseng rebelled at Xuzhou and dragged the province with him.

literal: Yan then made Lüe Grand Commander and ordered him to Pengcheng to receive and entice those newly submitting.
idiomatic: Yan made Lüe grand commander and sent him to Pengcheng to win new submits.

literal: When Lüe arrived he encamped south of the River; he was broken by Prince of Anle Jian and Lüe had only several tens of horse enter the city.
idiomatic: Lüe camped south of the River; Prince Jian of Anle routed him, and only a few dozen horsemen reached the city.

literal: Yan soon sent his Prince of Yuzhang Zong to hold Xuzhou and summoned Lüe and Faseng to return together.
idiomatic: Yan sent Prince Zong of Yuzhang to hold Xuzhou and recalled Lüe and Faseng.

literal: Though Lüe was in the southland, because of his family's calamity he wept morning and night, his body as if in mourning.
idiomatic: In the south he wept day and night for his family's ruin, living as in mourning.

literal: He also hated Faseng's character; in speaking with Faseng he never once smiled.
idiomatic: He despised Faseng and never smiled in his presence.

literal: Yan again appointed Lüe Hengzhou Inspector; he did not go.
idiomatic: Yan named him inspector of Hengzhou; he never went.
